cards.back: Resonance is the large response, a very big amplitude, that occurs when the **driving frequency** equals the natural frequency of the system.
cards.hint: Think about what happens to the amplitude as the driving frequency changes.

cards.front: How does a forced vibration differ from a free vibration in the frequency it vibrates at?
cards.back: A forced vibration vibrates at the **driving frequency**, set by the external force. A free vibration vibrates at its **natural frequency**, set by the system itself.
cards.hint: Compare what keeps pushing the system with what does not.

cards.front: What does lighter damping do to the shape of a resonance peak?
cards.back: Lighter damping makes the peak **taller and narrower**, because energy is lost more slowly so the amplitude can build up further.
cards.hint: Think about how quickly the energy drains away.

cards.front: What is the natural frequency of a system?
cards.back: The **natural frequency** is the frequency at which the system oscillates when it is disturbed and then left to vibrate freely.

cards.front: Why is the amplitude large when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency?
cards.back: The driver transfers energy most effectively at this frequency. Energy is added in every cycle, so the amplitude grows until the energy lost matches the energy supplied.
cards.hint: Think about how the driver's energy reaches the system each cycle.

cards.front: Why does the amplitude at resonance not keep growing without limit?
cards.back: Wrong idea: resonance makes the amplitude grow forever. Right: **energy losses** to the surroundings rise with amplitude and limit the size of the peak.

cards.front: What are the steps to produce an amplitude against driving frequency graph?
cards.back: 1. Keep the driving force constant. 2. Vary the driving frequency. 3. Measure the amplitude at each frequency. 4. Plot amplitude against driving frequency.

cards.front: What is the amplitude like at very low and very high driving frequencies?
cards.back: The amplitude is **small at both extremes**. It rises to a peak at $f_0$ and falls on both sides of that peak.
cards.hint: Picture the two ends of the resonance curve.

cards.front: What does critical damping do to a displaced system?
cards.back: It returns the system to equilibrium in the **shortest time without oscillating**, so it does not keep bouncing.
cards.hint: Compare this with a system that keeps swinging back and forth.

cards.back: **Damping** is the loss of energy from an oscillating system to its surroundings, which reduces the amplitude. Friction, air resistance and internal forces in materials all cause it.

cards.front: Name a situation where resonance is useful.
cards.back: Tuning a **radio circuit** to the frequency of one station, or pushing a swing in time with its natural motion.
cards.hint: Think of devices that pick out one frequency from many.

cards.front: Where is the peak of a heavily damped resonance curve centred, compared with $f_0$?
cards.back: It is centred **slightly below** $f_0$, and the peak is lower and broader than for light damping.
cards.hint: Compare this with the position of the lightly damped peak.

cards.front: Why does the amplitude of a free vibration gradually fall?
cards.back: Energy is lost to the surroundings, through **damping**, so the vibration dies away over time.
